title: STUDENT VOICE: Schools teach students what to learn, but rarely teach them how to learn
summary:
Schools spend years teaching algebra, chemistry and history to students. Yet too many finish high school without knowing how memory, attention and stress impact their learning. The post STUDENT VOICE: Schools teach students what to learn, but rarely teach them how to learn appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Schools spend years teaching algebra, chemistry and history to students. Yet too many finish high school without knowing how memory, attention and stress impact their learning. They assume that poor grades mean “they aren’t smart enough.”

The truth is, few students are taught evidence-backed strategies for studying, getting a good night’s sleep and managing stress before high-pressure exams.

If schools and teachers want students to thrive, they must teach them how to learn early on.

Case in point: My high school classmate pulled an all-nighter before an Advanced Placement U.S. History exam at Lithonia High School in metropolitan Atlanta, cramming Heimler’s History videos. During the test, he forgot much of the content he had studied. His conclusion was clear: “Maybe I should’ve studied harder.”

I disagreed. The issue wasn’t his effort. Nor his intelligence. It was that he had never been taught how learning worked.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education.

This is a significant issue for students in under-resourced communities, where access to guidance on how stress, sleep and attention affect learning is often limited.

Many students are left to figure out effective strategies on their own. I saw this firsthand at my school. It’s why I started the Cognition Club in ninth grade with the support of my counselor. As the club developed, we discussed foods that support concentration and strategies for managing stress while studying for the state-required Georgia Milestones Assessment — topics rarely addressed in class.

My interest in brain health came from home. My sister developed epilepsy when she was 9, and her grades slipped over time as it affected her memory, concentration and ability to attend school.

Witnessing how she often blamed herself for not doing as well as she had before, I gathered and gave her wellness and study strategies — such as good sleep hygiene, focused study intervals and techniques to reduce fatigue — drawing inspiration from Jim Kwik and Andrew Huberman.

These approaches helped her challenge the belief that her academic ability was fixed, and motivated her to pursue studies in business and law. While supporting her successful journey, I realized how simple methods can help students who doubt their ability to learn.

Eventually, our Cognition Club conversations shifted from how many hours we studied to how we studied. I noticed that students who initially treated the club as a study hall began to report less anxiety during tests.

Schools constantly assess learning through quizzes, assignments and standardized exams. Understanding how attention, stress and study habits affect learning can help students build stronger study routines, improve self-regulation and approach school and career paths with greater confidence. And for students navigating financial stress, family responsibilities or limited academic support, understanding how learning works can be especially valuable.

Related: Helping kids learn how their brains work

Entering higher education, I became increasingly aware that many students were not being introduced early enough to the science of learning. This motivated me to create NeuroPioneers Pathway in 2023 — an independent, student-led initiative focused on brain health education and mentorship for underserved middle and high school students.

Through curriculum development and educational outreach, I sought to introduce students to the relationship between everyday habits and learning, and to strategies to improve memory, attention and sleep. The experience reinforced my belief that young people should have opportunities to understand how their brains work before academic challenges begin to shape their confidence and limit their aspirations.

Many students assume that academic success is driven solely by hard work or innate ability. In our six-week curriculum in North Carolina, they gain exposure to brain health and protective habits through interactive workshops, hands-on learning and college student mentorship. They leave with a better understanding of how their habits affect their learning.

Teaching how attention and stress shape memory and learning is just as important as teaching academic content.

All students deserve to have opportunities to discover how their brains learn best, but schools don’t need to add another graduation requirement to make that happen. They can start by integrating basic learning-science concepts into existing health, science and advisory courses. A psychology teacher can host office hours or after-school meetings to help students study smarter, not harder. Social workers and guidance counselors can help students manage stressors for better focus on test day. School leaders can hold schoolwide assemblies to help students build better learning habits for academic success.

I’m not saying that teaching students about attention, stress, memory and effective study habits will solve every educational challenge. But it can help students better understand factors influencing their academic performance and help them learn more effectively.

Students shouldn’t have to discover successful habits through trial and error. If we want students to succeed, we’ve got to teach them not only what to learn, but also how learning works.

Victoria Ayodele is an undergraduate student studying neurological development and nutrition. Her interests include neuroscience education, brain health literacy and educational equity.

title: Colleges Say OPT Fee Would Cost Tens of Millions
summary:
Colleges Say OPT Fee Would Cost Tens of Millions
Johanna Alonso Wed, 11/11/2026 - 03:00 AM

A proposed fee would require colleges to pay at least $70,000 for each international graduate to work temporarily in the U.S. after graduation. Colleges say they can’t afford it—and foisting it onto students would create an unfair “pay-to-play” system.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
Colleges won’t be able to afford the Trump administration’s planned optional practical training fee, dozens of institutions wrote in public comments on the proposed rule. Many argued the fee would serve only to penalize students and institutions that are participating in OPT lawfully, rather than curb fraud—the administration’s stated goal.

The rule, which drew nearly 9,000 comments during a public comment period that closed Monday, is the latest salvo in the administration’s crusade against international students and pathways for those students to work in the U.S. Optional practical training has historically allowed international students to temporarily work in the U.S. after graduation; it was expanded by President George W. Bush in 2008. But conservatives have criticized the program for supposedly taking jobs from American workers. In the rule, the Department of Homeland Security also cited fraud schemes, in which international students claim to work at companies that don’t exist to stay in the U.S., as part of its rationale for the new fee.

But colleges and their advocates questioned why the department believes the fee will have the intended effect and how it decided upon the amount, which is $70,000 for an initial application and $30,000 for subsequent applications. DHS has previously proposed a $100,000 fee for individuals on H-1B visas, which are used by highly skilled foreign workers.

The American Council on Education noted that the fee could even encourage fraud.

“The new fee creates a new ‘pay-to-play’ structure for OPT because previously it was available to any qualified international student completing studies at a U.S. institution. This new fee does not help distinguish between a responsible institution and a qualified student and appears to punish institutions that follow the rules,” the organization wrote in its comment. “Highly skilled, law-abiding international graduates who lack the financial ability to pay tens of thousands of dollars for OPT will be pushed to the margins and unable to access this program.”

But regardless of whether the fee will offset fraud, it’s certain to decrease the number of students who can lawfully participate in OPT, as institutions would have to pay millions that they don’t have to continue funding applications at the rate they currently submit them.

An analysis of comments from Association of American Universities member institutions found that not even the nation’s more resourced research institutions feel they could afford the fees. Of those who both submitted comments and provided an estimate of how much they would pay annually, the lowest was Tulane University, which would have to foot a $13 million bill each year. On the high end, eight institutions would owe over $100 million annually, including Arizona State University, which hosts the most international students of any U.S. university.

(The analysis includes only comments that had been uploaded to the Federal Register by midday Tuesday.)

In the rule, DHS estimated the total cost to institutions would be between $8.7 billion and $16.9 billion. For just those 22 AAU members, the total annual cost is estimated at about $2.1 billion.

The institutions all said they wouldn’t be able to pay. Some, like the University of Kansas, noted that the cost would be more than they bring in each year in tuition from international students.

But it’s not just major research institutions that would face the brunt of OPT fees. In their public comments, smaller institutions with substantial international populations pointed out how difficult it would be to afford the costs. Lewis University, a private Lasallian university with 7,000 students, 870 of whom are international, estimated that its annual OPT fees would equal $46.8 million—a whopping 30 percent of its annual operating budget.

“An OPT fee structure this high would render OPT options for any Lewis international students virtually impossible,” wrote Tyler King, executive director of international affairs, and Angela M. Rodriguez, director of International Student and Global Scholar Services.

Institutions also said it was unlikely they could push those fees off onto students or employers, both because it’s highly unlikely students and employers could afford such costs and because it wouldn’t be fair. Some institutions noted that other students are not forced to pay to get work or internship experience, and the University of Minnesota said it would go against its “access mandate as a public institution” to force the fee onto students. It would also mean only high-income international students have access to job training.

Similarly, colleges argued that there would be no adequate way to select which students should be allowed to participate in OPT out of multiple equally qualified graduates.

“Lewis views all of its graduates as employment-ready, so it would be unethical and unfair to choose only a few international graduates for OPT eligibility,” King and Rodriguez wrote.

If the rule were to go into effect and force institutions to stop offering students access to OPT, or significantly roll it back, the repercussions could be far-reaching.

Because OPT is a major motivator for international students coming to the U.S., the fee could likely cause international enrollment, already on the decline, to plummet further. Institutions and their advocates noted that those declines would impact not only the institutions but also the local and national economies, which international student contribute billions to, as well as research and innovation in the U.S. Research has indicated that STEM OPT workers spur new companies and patents.

Students themselves said in their comments that they had come to the U.S. in part to pursue OPT and argued that the fee would completely blindside currently enrolled international students.

“I budgeted carefully for tuition, housing, and living costs before I ever boarded a plane. A $70,000 fee for OPT was never part of that math because no reasonable person could have anticipated it,” wrote one anonymous commenter who identified themself as a current international student. “Imposing it now pulls the rug out from under students who made life-altering decisions in good faith under the rules as they existed. We cannot retroactively un-spend years of tuition or un-choose the country where we studied. A policy change this extreme, applied to students already enrolled, is simply unfair—it punishes people for failing to predict the unpredictable.”

Numerous professors also reported that their labs would be severely impacted and graduate programs at their institutions could shutter without international students.

Emily E. Scott, a professor of pharmacy at the University of Michigan whose work centers around how specific enzymes help the body process medicines, noted that she has several postdoctoral researchers work in her lab under OPT.

“In experimental research, it takes time to learn a technique well enough to troubleshoot an experiment and interpret the results with confidence,” she wrote. “As postdocs gain that experience, they can take on more responsibility and help move projects forward. If the fees lead universities to make fewer OPT recommendations, labs like mine will have fewer opportunities to bring in researchers with the right scientific background. When a position goes unfilled, the experiments that depend on that person’s work can be delayed.”

Another professor, François Blanchette of the University of California, Merced, called it a “colossal waste of all the efforts that went into training these students” to disallow them to work in the U.S. after graduation.

“The progress of American science would be hindered, while that of other countries would be hastened,” Blanchette wrote. “In the long run, an excellent strategy to weaken another country is to entice their best minds to move to the US. This policy does exactly the opposite and instead weakens the US.”

The comments supporting the rule largely focused on concern that graduates using OPT are taking jobs from American workers. One commenter named Jolene Christopherson said that, with the rise of artificial intelligence, “we need to focus on our ability to train and give jobs to citizens of the U.S.” Another said that, over his years working in the tech industry, “I’ve seen how OPT and other programs like it displace American workers.”

Many supportive commenters said they felt the rule wasn’t harsh enough and that they wished for the administration to eliminate OPT entirely.

Institutions, in contrast, called on DHS to toss the rule and urged the department to find a more evidence-based way to combat fraud.

title: Second Harvard Union Goes on Strike
summary:
Second Harvard Union Goes on Strike
Emma Whitford Wed, 11/11/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
The union representing more than 2,500 non-tenure-track researchers, postdocs and contingent faculty at Harvard University went on strike Tuesday after more than two years of bargaining with university officials for their first contract. Harvard Academic Workers are now the second striking union at the university, following the Harvard Graduate Student Union, which walked off the job on Oct. 27.

“We don’t want to strike, but Harvard’s administration has left us no choice. After two years of frozen wages and protracted negotiations, along with high inflation and endowment growth of over ten billion dollars, Harvard is still refusing to compensate us fairly for the value we provide to the University. The Harvard Corporation needs to do better, and thousands of workers across campus are standing strong together to send them that message,” Nick Colella, core research staff, said in a news release.

Harvard Academic Workers remain at odds with administrators over wages; childcare and family benefits; and discrimination, harassment and bullying protections. Harvard officials most recently offered the union 3.5 percent raises and 1 percent ratification bonus, according to the union release. For its part, the union has proposed raises ranging from 7 percent to 12 percent, depending on what workers are currently earning, plus 5 percent raise minimums for promotions and annual cost of living and “longevity” increases.

Harvard spokespeople did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

title: After the Election, a Chance to Correct Our Course
summary:
After the Election, a Chance to Correct Our Course
Elizabeth Redden Wed, 11/11/2026 - 03:00 AM

For colleges that have acceded to unwarranted or unlawful political demands, now is the time to reclaim institutional independence.

Byline(s)
Suzanne Nossel
full_text:
When Texas A&M University’s spring semester began in January, a philosophy professor was told to remove passages from Plato’s Symposium or teach a different course. Professor Leonard Bright’s graduate seminar on ethics in public policy was canceled after its first meeting. The incidents resulted from policies adopted by the Texas A&M System Board of Regents restricting how faculty could teach about race and gender. Roughly 200 arts and sciences courses were affected.

On Election Day, Texas voters ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, electing Gina Hinojosa in the first election of a Democratic governor since 1990. The election will not automatically restore the Plato readings to the syllabus. But it presents an opening for university leaders who have spent years accommodating inappropriate and sometimes unlawful political demands to reclaim the independence they are entrusted to safeguard.

The Democrats’ midterm triumph has transformed the political landscape in Washington and beyond. In Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, voters replaced Republican governors with Democrats. Democrats also captured both legislative chambers in Wisconsin and flipped the Houses in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, plus the Pennsylvania Senate, among other gains. Twenty-two states now have Democratic trifectas, with Democrats controlling both legislative chambers and the governor’s office. These shifts offer universities new political allies and, in some states, a path toward reversing policies that have curtailed academic freedom and institutional autonomy.

In another sign of changes afoot, Harmeet Dhillon, the Trump administration’s assistant attorney general for civil rights, resigned her post last week. Dhillon spearheaded investigations of universities over admissions, diversity policies and allegations of antisemitism. Her tactics helped turn the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, historically a bulwark against discrimination, into an instrument of ideological pressure on American higher education.

While higher education was not a leading ballot issue, voters’ repudiation of Trumpian rule should nonetheless prompt a reckoning within university leadership. The political pressures that led some presidents and trustees to make costly concessions and accept intrusive federal oversight are shifting. With the Trump administration’s political leverage diminished, university submission to government coercion must also subside, lest it become an enduring feature of American higher education.

Since Trump’s return to office, universities have faced an extraordinary campaign of federal intimidation. Billions of dollars in research funding were frozen, student visas threatened and civil rights investigations wielded as leverage to compel changes in institutional policies and leadership. Allegations of wrongdoing became grounds for demanding settlements before any adjudication of the underlying claims.

Courts have repeatedly found the administration’s tactics illegal. In September 2025, a federal judge ruled that the termination of more than $2 billion in research grants to Harvard University violated federal law and the university’s First Amendment rights. The judge concluded that antisemitism had served as a pretext for sweeping demands aimed at bringing Harvard into ideological conformity. The administration has appealed. Separate court orders also blocked Trump’s efforts to bar international students from Harvard.

Other institutions chose negotiation over litigation, afraid to take on a vindictive and powerful government. By this fall, at least seven prominent universities had entered into agreements of varying scope with the administration, including Brown, Columbia, Cornell and Northwestern Universities; the Universities of Pennsylvania and Virginia; and, most recently, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Four of these institutions committed a combined $406 million in payments and designated spending, without a court judgment establishing liability. The policy concessions are at least as consequential. Columbia agreed to a comprehensive review of its Middle East–related academic programs, including leadership and curriculum. Brown accepted federal definitions of sex for women’s athletics and specified housing provisions. And just last month, UNC Chapel Hill agreed to federal restrictions on admissions and recruitment partnerships, including prohibitions affecting certain programs designed to help students from underrepresented groups gain access to college.

University leaders have insisted that their settlements preserve academic autonomy and largely reaffirm existing obligations and commitments. Presidents and trustees argue that they protected research programs, employees and students from potentially devastating losses and disruptions.

University leaders faced difficult choices, with the livelihoods of researchers and the future of lifesaving work hanging in the balance. Institutions without Harvard’s financial resources could reasonably fear the consequences of prolonged confrontation.

But the contention that little of substance was conceded does not hold up to scrutiny. If a university has done nothing wrong, paying tens of millions of dollars to end an investigation smacks of extortion. If admissions or curriculum changes were already justified, they should not have happened via talks undertaken under financial duress. Even if understandable, universities’ decisions to submit undermine their role as vital, autonomous institutions of civic life in a democracy.

Changes to university life have spread well beyond the short list of prominent institutions that signed on the dotted lines. Others have changed policies, pared back support for diversity efforts and policed curriculum to avoid attracting negative scrutiny. University leaders need to own up to the fact that such accommodations normalize an approach whereby political officials—both overtly and tacitly—threaten independent institutions into accepting government-defined ideological constraints.

Universities now have an opportunity and an imperative to correct course. Universities contemplating concessions should stiffen their spines and resist the threats and the arm-twisting. Those that have changed policies should distinguish changes reflecting genuine institutional judgments from those made due to coercion. Existing legal commitments must be honored, but apart from those obligations, institutions should resist interpretations that restrict inquiry or campus life. Government has a legitimate role in enforcing civil rights laws. But its authority to investigate discrimination does not confer a license to dictate a university’s intellectual or social life.

The state-level election results create additional possibilities. In Texas, Gov.-elect Hinojosa will have opportunities to reshape university governing boards through appointments. In Ohio, Gov.-elect Amy Acton can challenge the restrictive approach embodied in Senate Bill 1, which imposed sweeping controls over DEI programs and university governance. The new Texas House majority and newly Democratic chambers in North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin can scrutinize state policies that have subordinated institutional decision-making to political priorities. Repealing existing laws will require legislative action, but the space for resistance and reconsideration has expanded.

None of this suggests universities should reverse legitimate reforms undertaken during these difficult years. Campus antisemitism demands serious treatment. Admissions practices must comply with applicable judicial rulings, which prohibit race-conscious admissions. Debates over viewpoint diversity, faculty heterogeneity and the right approaches to diversity and inclusion should be shaped by academic expertise, student perspectives and public accountability, not by a sword of political peril dangling over the campus.

Some institutions demonstrated that resistance was possible. Harvard went to court. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology helped lead the rejection of the administration’s proposed “compact” for higher education in 2025, emboldening other universities to follow suit. But over all, rather than uniting in defense of the principles of free expression and open inquiry for which they stand, universities have run scared and scattered.

The new Congress will not take office until January, and President Trump will retain substantial executive authority. Universities should harbor no illusions that political intimidation has ended. Their independence must rest on convictions and structures sturdy enough to withstand pressure from any political quarter.

The universities that negotiated their way through the last two years may have protected important interests in the short term. They also risked teaching Washington that draconian threats would bring even the country’s most prestigious institutions to heel.

University presidents should use this electoral turning point to convey a different lesson. Their institutions answer to the law and to the public interest, but their academic missions belong to the communities entrusted with fulfilling them. Just as voters have pivoted, so should university leaders abandon their defensive crouch and stand up together in defense of the institutions they lead and the values they represent.

title: Let’s Not Blame Faculty for What They Haven’t Had to Know
summary:
Let’s Not Blame Faculty for What They Haven’t Had to Know
rachel.toor Wed, 11/11/2026 - 03:00 AM

Rachel schools Gordon on not being a clear and transparent communicator with the faculty.

Byline(s)
Rachel Toor
E. Gordon Gee
full_text:
RST: Are you still mad at me, Gordon? On the phone the other day, you said it was the twins’ 14th birthday. You got all grandfather proud and texted me a photo of you holding both of them as newborns. I made barfing sounds and said they looked like mushrooms.

EGG: I am not mad, although I have taken you out of the will.

RST: Moving along, do you think the last two crazy years are a blip in U.S. history and things are going to be more sane now? I am embracing optimism on all fronts.

EGG: Embrace optimism. Our democracy is very strong and resilient and last week was the proof. The Dems will probably overplay their hand, but that is fine because the R’s have done that over the past two years. Maybe we can finally find ourselves perched in the middle of our electorate. That is my hope.

RST: Here’s something that caught me off guard at a recent conference: I was talking about how little attention faculty pay to the national landscape of higher ed and often don’t realize that their campus problems are actually pretty darned universal. Most faculty don’t read The Chronicle or Inside Higher Ed. An administrator stopped me and said, “That’s because we told them they didn’t have to. They focused on their students and their disciplines and their campuses because that’s how we reward them.”

EGG: Rachel, you are right. As I have been working on this project with you, I have discovered that I am not certain that I truly understand faculty. I have lived in rarefied air for most of my academic life, and I find the daily toil of a faculty member often a mystery. So, it is easy to get irritated with faculty because I expect them to know the issues of the day. Yet, as you just said, I spent much of my life telling them not to worry, just do your jobs and let me do mine. In another time and place that may have worked, but now, given the challenges facing universities of all stripes, I should have been communicating regularly about the challenges the whole sector was facing.

RST: Every president I know thinks they are communicating regularly with the faculty. Most say they are transparent. I’ve heard you tell current presidents that they have to be better at this, but how good were you?

EGG: Not good enough. I decided that we needed to go through a process of academic transformation at West Virginia due to a $45 million structural deficit. The reason to immediately address the problem was absolutely clear to me, but it was a bolt out of the blue to most of our faculty. In retrospect, I should have been preparing people for at least a year, because I knew what was happening at so many institutions and we were not immune. Bad news is hard to deliver, but it is better to keep faculty informed rather than hope for a miracle.

RST: And now you wear that no-confidence vote proudly, along with your Ted Lasso BELIEVE lapel pin.😊 But I don’t think this was just you. Presidents know this stuff is happening elsewhere but somehow believe it won’t land on them. Did you really not know, or did you not want to face the facts and make the hard decisions? How does a giant budget gap just appear?

EGG: I could feel it coming. Everything changed after COVID, and we were losing students at an unexpected rate. I felt we could grow our student body based on the classes that we had during my first few years. Although I was accused during our transformation for budgeting for 40,000 students as a reason for our deficit, we did not budget based on ghost numbers. I may be a risk taker, but I never budgeted on hope. With COVID, it was apparent that we were going to have a deficit.

RST: Were you surprised by the reaction of the faculty? Did you expect them to have been paying attention to what was going on elsewhere?

EGG: Actually, I was surprised. I naively thought that people would be reading the news that showed the financial precarity of institutions. The bond agencies started lowering ratings for universities and colleges, which scared the hell out of me. These agencies have a cadre of very smart people measuring trends, and they were signaling that the sector was in real trouble.

RST: Look. I’ve been reading The Chronicle since 1984 and writing for it since 1997, and until I started talking to presidents nearly four years ago, I had no idea how much I didn’t understand about higher ed, especially about budgeting. And yet, until recently, that hasn’t stopped me from blaming faculty colleagues for not knowing stuff I didn’t know until I had to learn.

EGG: It certainly did not stop me or members of my senior team from wondering on what planet people were living. It is easy for the faculty in times of stress to blame the administration. But what was actually startling to me was how fast the leaders of the university were critical of the faculty. In earlier times during my presidencies, I had not experienced so much animosity and finger-pointing from both sides.

RST: You, my friend, have been quite critical of faculty, which is one of our common themes. But the truth is, we need to be taught. I still don’t understand a lot of the higher ed news I read. There was a headline about “pocket rescissions” and I had to ask people what that meant. Reporters and others talk about “neg reg” and I’m like, Huh? And all the policies referred to by acronyms? I’m lost. It’s impossible to keep up with the news and we all cherry-pick the stuff that pertains to us, so we miss a lot of big-picture issues. As a faculty member, I would like a readable, informative (nutritious as well as delicious) summary of what’s going on that will have implications on my specific campus. And the fact is, that is nowhere to be found. Should it come from the office of the president?

EGG: Given the divisions which are occurring on campus, it needs to come from a credible source that all parties in the university believe is/are straight shooters and who also have the ability to make the information simple and readable.

RST: But it has to be specific, because, as I’ve been trying to teach you, each niche of the ecosystem has both similar and distinct issues. Remember what you learned at Hendrix College?

EGG: Truly, Rachel, although this is an important discussion, it is actually quite painful for me. I have learned to park issues that have bothered me and move on. Saying that, this notion of conflict between faculty and administration is such a debilitating reality within universities. If I could go back with the knowledge I have now, I would make different choices. Chief among them would be to bury fear and be very clear with every conversation and decision that there is a rationale based upon all of the information the university is providing. In other words, as part of shared governance, I would provide all of the appropriate information to the university family, and if they read and listened then they would clearly understand the status of the university and challenges facing the higher education sector. Failure to do this has caused me a lot of heartburn, and for many of my colleague presidents, it has caused them to be fired or resign.

RST: Yep. Here’s something else I’ve been thinking a lot about: When you look at who is talking about what higher ed needs to do and how it must change, it’s often outside observers. Someone recently pointed out that a big name in the industry gets a lot of money for going around talking about what has to happen and that person has never worked inside higher ed (and no, I’m not talking about IHE co-founder Doug Lederman). So we have pundits, former journalists and a whole industry of consultants who have never been responsible for a course, sat through a department meeting or prepared a tenure file talking about faculty. And we also have a bunch of old former presidents beating up on their peers still in the job and the faculty who beat up on them. Where are the sane, informed voices?

EGG: US! Truthfully, is that not what we are trying to do with the Odd Couple? We can provide informed opinions and observations about higher education from two people who have been deep in the trenches. And, yes, there are a lot of commentators flapping their lips about higher education who have never spent a day in the seat of a faculty or administrator. Yet they are expounding on the world of higher education as if they fully understand all of the nuances of the most complex organizations in this country. They often do more harm than good.

RST: Well, Gordon, no one is going to listen to us if you just complain about the faculty being whiny (yes, calling you out because you’ve said this a zillion times and often in all caps) and if you give a bunch of generic advice and rules for current presidents to follow. BTW, I’m still hearing about how you said that when you came in as president the first thing you did was fire the provost because you knew that person wanted your job. That might have been true in your specific context, but it sure as shooting isn’t universally the case.

EGG: I respect faculty, and certainly individually I have found so many friends over these five institutions. Saying that, in my conversations with university presidents, there is a common theme about faculty resistance to change. The net result is that there always is a lot of noise in the system.

RST: And some of the noise is coming from the pundit class. I’ve had to point out to Doug just how much he has missed about higher ed. The other day I complained to him about how hard it was to schedule a meeting with just a handful of concerned faculty members. Doug said, “Oh yeah. That was a funny bit in Vladimir!” He hadn’t known after all those years covering higher ed what things are like on the ground. And to his credit, Doug 2.0 is learning.

EGG: You are always trying to take credit for helping older guys who may have lost a little bit of their fastball.

RST: It’s a dirty job, but. What I’m grappling with now is how we expect people to understand the sector if there’s no general interest publication for faculty, except for whatever comes out of AAUP (I’m not a member, so I don’t know what they’re saying, though I can guess), and no substantive communications coming from their own administrations.

EGG: Look, the last thing I want to be is one of the arrogant people who believe that they are the only ones who understand the issues and therefore have the corner on all of the wisdom. But there is a reality about higher education which is that it is very complex, messy with so many variations from large and small, public and private, Mormon and Catholic. Take me, for example: What I am learning from you and this journey that we are pursuing is how much I do not know about higher education.

title: Colleges report declines in international enrollment amid federal restrictions
summary: Survey data released Wednesday found that nearly 6 in 10 U.S. colleges lost foreign graduate students this fall, and 45% saw a decline in undergraduates.
full_text:
Dive Brief:

Nearly 6 out of 10 colleges reported a drop in international graduate students in fall 2026, compared to the previous year, with an average decline of 13%, according to a new survey of 203 U.S. higher education institutions. Some 45% also said they had fewer foreign undergraduates enroll.

The data, released Wednesday, found that 90% of respondents cited restrictive federal policies as being a significant obstacle to international enrollment. Just under half, 47%, also said tuition and living costs for students posed a significant barrier.

Surveyed colleges also expressed dismal expectations for next year, with 44% predicting international enrollment would stay at the same depressed levels and 37% expecting enrollment to decline further.

Dive Insight:

Wednesday’s survey, released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators in partnership with the Oxford University Press and the student recruitment platform Studyportals, reinforces concerns that the Trump administration's attacks on foreign students and the long-standing U.S. programs that support their study here would corrode the international enrollment pipeline.

Survey respondents cited the administration’s crackdown on student visas and the astronomical new fees sought for the H-1B visa and Optional Practical Training programs. While some of those policies are being challenged in the courts, they can signal to international students that they are unwelcome in the U.S., and the uncertainty and instability can ward off prospective applicants.

Major public research universities, traditionally popular among foreign students, have begun reporting international enrollment declines this fall. And some, like Pennsylvania State University, have drawn a direct line between that loss of students and budgetary challenges.

“These survey results affirm what we’ve observed before: national policies matter to international students making major decisions about where to study, conduct research, or start a career,” Fanta Aw, NAFSA’s executive director and CEO, said in a statement Wednesday.

Some colleges also reported decreased interest in countries that have historically sent the most higher education students overseas, such as China and India.

“Our agents in India in particular are telling us that they are seeing a drastic decline in inquiries for US graduate study and that many prospective students are either considering other destinations or postponing study plans,” one university respondent said.

Of those surveyed, 37% of U.S. colleges said they planned to diversify the locations where they recruit from and tap into new markets over the next 12 months.

One institution said it would pivot to the Philippines, Canada and Colombia as a means of offsetting losses from India, Bangladesh and Nepal, the three countries from which the college traditionally got the most foreign students.

Another 32% said they would expand their online offerings, and 30% said they would turn to budget cuts.

However, cuts could further exacerbate challenges for colleges’ international admissions offices. One respondent admitted that staffing issues have “resulted in a lack of attention to incoming students.”

title: Researchers and faculty sue NSF over axing of its social science unit
summary: The federal agency said it would close the unit in fiscal 2027, in what the lawsuit described as a unilateral decision that violated Administrative Procedure Act.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

A coalition of academic researchers, scientists, instructors, graduate students and university departments on Monday sued the National Science Foundation over its decision to shutter its Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences Directorate.

In their lawsuit, the plaintiffs allege that NSF leadership violated the Administrative Procedure Act and the statute creating the agency by unilaterally announcing in April it would eliminate the directorate, known as SBE, in fiscal year 2027.

The decision to end SBE and its hundreds of millions in research funding is reckless and illegal and would “devastate social, behavioral, and economic sciences in the United States,” the complaint said. The plaintiffs are asking the court to reverse NSF’s decision and block the closure. The agency did not immediately respond to questions on Monday.

Dive Insight:

Since April, NSF has “stopped funding opportunities for basic SBE research,” reassigned almost all of SBE's staff and cut ties with scientists who were working with the directorate, according to Monday’s lawsuit.

President Donald Trump also fired every member of SBE’s governing board, who plaintiffs said had been kept in the dark about the agency’s future since he retook office almost two years ago.

Their lawsuit argued that NSF breached the APA by failing to consider the outcome of doing away with SBE — namely, that the agency would be unable to fulfill its mandate to “initiate and support basic scientific research and programs” in the social sciences.

Each year, SBE distributes some $247 million in grants for research into the social, behavioral and economic sciences — nearly two-thirds of all federal grants in these fields, according to NSF.

“Without that funding, hundreds of promising research projects directed to the pressing problems of our time — from the use and effects of artificial intelligence to child development in the age of social media — will never proceed,” the lawsuit said. Thousands of people also will lose their jobs, it said.

The plaintiffs also said NSF has given no official rationale for why it decided to extinguish the directorate.

In response to questions from The Atlantic, a White House spokesperson said in a May statement that the Trump administration “is committed to cementing America’s dominance in cutting-edge technologies of the future — innovation that is being driven by advancements in hard sciences, not in ideologically-driven ‘social sciences.’”

But the administration never said why it is labeling entire fields such as psychology and economics as “ideologically driven,” the plaintiffs said in their lawsuit Monday. And even if it were to explain, they argued, the rationale would directly conflict with the statutes that created NSF, “which repeatedly direct the Foundation to support the social sciences.”

All of this has occurred with a significant power vacuum at the top levels of NSF. The agency has been without a permanent leader for more than a year and a half, after its last director, Sethuraman Panchanathan, resigned in April 2025. It is also without a deputy director.

Both positions require a presidential appointment and Senate confirmation. Trump’s pick for NSF director, former U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Deputy Secretary Jim O'Neill, has not been given a confirmation hearing.

NSF Chief of Staff Brian Stone, a defendant in Monday’s lawsuit, is currently performing the duties of the agency’s director. The vast majority of NSF's significant cuts and the corresponding tumult occurred during Stone’s tenure. He is set to retire at the end of the year.

“NSF cannot shut down the government’s largest source of funding for an entire scientific sector without a Director and without consulting the body Congress created to make such Decisions,” Monday’s lawsuit said. “And it certainly cannot do so with no explanation.”

title: Cabo Verde’s presidential election: the stakes in one of Africa’s most stable democracies
summary: The presidential election will test party loyalties and voters’ expectations of the presidency, as well as its role in the political system.
full_text:
Cape Verde’s presidential election takes place against the backdrop of a democratic record that remains unusual in its regional context. The country, made up of an archipelago of islands off the coast of west Africa, has sustained multiparty competition for more than three decades. It has had peaceful transfers of power and no coups or military takeovers since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Cabo Verde (population 530,000) is a semi-presidential republic in which the president is directly elected. The prime minister is appointed by the president in light of parliamentary election results, and heads a government that is politically accountable to the national assembly.

The president represents the state and safeguards the constitution, while the prime minister and the government conduct public policy.

The presidency nevertheless carries substantial political weight. The president can veto legislation, request constitutional review and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. The office also entails responsibilities in foreign affairs and national defence.

The president is, therefore, not the principal policymaker. However, the way in which these powers are exercised can become particularly consequential when the president and prime minister belong to opposing political camps. This might indeed be the outcome of the 15 November 2026 election.

I am a political communication specialist who has researched the dynamics of Cabo Verde’s presidential elections. In my view the central test for the upcoming poll will be whether the country’s institutions can continue to function effectively while preserving the important distinction between the presidency and the government.

The background

Cape Verde’s political climate is shaped by a recent change of government. The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde returned to office after winning the May 2026 parliamentary election. This ended 10 years of government by the Movement for Democracy, which now forms the opposition.

The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde’s victory reflected growing voter dissatisfaction with a decade of rule by the Movement for Democracy. This is particularly over poor inter-island transport, economic difficulties, living conditions and public security.

The change of government renewed questions about the balance of power between the president, the new government and parliament, as well as the opposition’s ability to hold the ruling party accountable.

The forthcoming presidential election will, therefore, test not only party loyalties but also voters’ expectations of the presidency and its role in the political system.

The two main contenders are José Maria Neves, backed by the African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde, and Joana Rosa, supported by the Movement for Democracy.

Neves previously served as prime minister between 2001 and 2016. Rosa, a former minister of justice, is the first woman to run for president in Cabo Verde.

They face Antero Tavares, Casimiro de Pina, Gilson Alves and Loisito Sousa. These four offer alternatives to the two parties that have dominated national politics since the introduction of multipartyism in 1991.

These candidates are unlikely, however, to attract support on a scale that would challenge the two main contenders.

The voters

Together with political science researchers Danielton Delgado and Susana Rogeiro Nina, I published a paper that offers insight into the dynamics of presidential elections in Cabo Verde. Our 2019 study found that voters didn’t consistently use presidential contests to punish the governing party. Indeed, except in 2011 and 2021, every presidential election in the country was won by the candidate backed by the party that controlled parliament and the executive.

Also, there was not a systematic advantage for independent candidates or candidates backed by smaller parties. The short interval – one to six months – between legislative and presidential elections may help explain this phenomenon, as presidential contests often take place during the governing party’s post-election “honeymoon period”.

What’s different in the upcoming election?

If Neves secures re-election, the presidency and government will be held by figures associated with the same party. This possibility is not unlikely. Since the introduction of multiparty democracy in 1991, every incumbent president who has sought a second term has been re-elected: António Mascarenhas Monteiro in 1996, Pedro Pires in 2006 and Jorge Carlos Fonseca in 2016.

A victory for Neves could play out in one of two ways. It could facilitate cooperation, but it could also raise questions about the president’s independence from the government.

In turn, a victory for Rosa, mirroring the patterns that emerged in 2011 and 2021, would create a situation of divided leadership, with a Movement for Democracy-backed president working alongside an African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde government.

Such an arrangement is not inherently problematic. Nevertheless, it can require negotiation when constitutional responsibilities and political interests diverge.

Cabo Verde has recent experience of this situation: between November 2021 and the formation of the new government in June 2026, Neves dealt with a Movement for Democracy government. This was led by Ulisses Correia e Silva. Despite their partisan differences, relations were generally characterised by institutional cooperation rather than open confrontation.

In short, whoever wins will face a distinct institutional challenge. Neves will have to balance his party affiliation with the constitutional responsibility to act as head of state. Rosa will need to establish a working relationship with a government led by her political opponents.

title: ‘Treasures for the entire planet’: Scientists map life in one of the world’s last wild ecosystems
summary: Scientists are mapping one of the world’s last wild ecosystems to help us ‘understand what we have lost elsewhere’.
full_text:
Nesting turtles, fish-filled coral reefs, and mysterious deep-sea creatures: this is what scientists found in one of the world’s last largely untouched ecosystems.

Two remote coral atolls in the Pacific Ocean are being studied to support local and global conservation efforts.

Bikar and Bokak became the Marshall Islands’ first national marine sanctuaries in 2025. Since then, scientists have been working to establish a comprehensive ecological baseline for the 48,000-square-kilometre site, from sky to land and sea.

Their findings matter far beyond the remote atolls, which lie around 116 and 385 kilometres from the nearest inhabited atoll, respectively.

Related

“They are among the best ecological reference systems we have to better understand what we have lost elsewhere and to provide fundamental insights needed for effective conservation and restoration efforts,” says marine ecologist Dr Alan Friedlander of the University of Hawai’i.

He served as chief scientist aboard a joint expedition in Bikar and Bokak with Pristine Seas, a global conservation and exploration project founded by National Geographic Explorer Enric Sala to help protect vital ocean areas.

What they found were “some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region” – and perhaps the world.

‘Treasures for the entire planet’: What the world can learn from remote ecosystems

Extensive monitoring of Bikar and Bokak in 2023 informed the creation of the protected area.

Researchers were guided by the Marshall Islands’ national framework for community-led conservation, which seeks to protect natural resources “while ensuring island life thrives for generations to come”, explains Friedlander, who led a recent study on the atolls’ ecosystems.

“Bikar and Bokak are not just treasures for the Marshall Islands but for the entire planet, a gift from the community of Utirik Atoll, which has traditionally and vigilantly safeguarded these fragile ecosystems for decades,” he says.

While the atolls have recently gained national protection, they have long been cared for through community-led stewardship, with high chiefs establishing ‘mo’ or ‘taboo’ areas. In these zones, human activity is restricted, allowing nature to rest and replenish – an approach that has been incorporated into the national framework.

It has resulted in an ecosystem that offers an unparalleled glimpse into how life functions with only minimal human influence.

“The Marshall Island government should be applauded for their foresight in protecting these global biodiversity hotspots, where human activity is distant and habitats teem with life,” says Friedlander. “As human activities increasingly threaten biodiversity, areas devoid of intense human impacts serve as vital refugia.”

Large marine protected areas like these are globally important benchmarks for understanding how tropical ocean ecosystems are structured and how they may change in an era shaped by human activity, the researchers say.

Remote atolls teem with life while wildlife is in decline elsewhere

Bikar and Bokak offer a rare contrast to most of the world. Monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73 per cent globally since 1970, according to WWF’s 2026 Living Planet Report, with marine populations down 59 per cent.

Bleaching-level heat stress hit 84 per cent of the world’s coral reefs between January 2023 and May 2025, and only around 3.5 per cent of the ocean is considered fully or highly protected.

Using scuba, underwater video, deep-sea cameras, and a submarine, Pristine Seas scientists explored Pacific ecosystems that, by contrast, remain relatively intact.

Across both atolls, they found 15 breeding or likely breeding seabird species and more than 260 kinds of reef fish, as well as open-water predators including sharks, jacks and wahoo. Cameras and a submarine also revealed “surprisingly diverse and poorly known deep-sea communities”, and two of the fish recorded might be new to science, the researchers say.

Nesting green sea turtles were also observed at Bikar.

Ecological differences between the two reefs were noted, although the researchers say the reasons are not yet clear. Bokak’s reefs are dominated by coral, with around twice the fish biomass of Bikar, where seaweed covers more than half of some deeper slopes.

The project also highlights the importance of assessing ecosystems in their entirety in order to conserve their integrity and track future climate-driven change, the researchers say, adding that future studies should examine nutrient transfer and ecological connectivity between habitats.

title: International business student decline could cost UK economy £4.2bn
summary:
The UK economy could experience a £4.2 billion loss if international business students' numbers continue to fall and return to their 2019/20 level, a new report reveals.

The post International business student decline could cost UK economy £4.2bn appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Representing a 30% drop in enrolments, this economic loss is equivalent to 32,300 jobs. The report, carried out by London Economics for the Chartered Association of Business Schools, analysed international students’ economic contributions to the UK economy.

It found that since the tightening of immigration measures, such as the visa ban for student dependents, international business school enrolments have already fallen by 18% following their peak in 2022/23.

This decline in students reflects a loss of £600m to higher education providers and £2.1bn to the wider UK economy. If enrolments continue to follow this trend, substantial impacts on the economy, higher education and jobs will be seen.

A reduction of just 11% between 2024/25 and 2029/30 would result in a £1.7bn loss in net economic impact. This is equivalent to 12,100 jobs – roughly the number of people working at London Stansted Airport.

Meanwhile, international business school students are predicted to contribute billions to the UK economy over the duration of their studies, according to the data.

Recent declines in international student numbers have already cost the country billions

Michael Mainelli, Chartered ABS International Students Taskforce

“Business schools are engines of economic growth,” said Michael Mainelli, chair of the Chartered ABS International Students Taskforce.

“This report demonstrates the value of international business school students and the vital role they play in local economies across the country. Yet recent declines in international student numbers have already cost the country billions,” he added.

With around one in three UK international students enrolled in a Business school, more than any other subject area, their contributions to the economy are significant.

Each student generates, on average, around £103,000 for the UK economy during their time in the UK.

The report found that £16.8bn in gross economic benefits will be generated from the 148,500 students who began Business and Management courses in 2024/25.

After deducting approximately £1.5bn in public service costs, their contribution to the UK economy amounts to £15.3bn. This represents almost 40% of the £40.4bn net economic benefit that will be brought in by all international students that year.

This economic impact is estimated to have supported 107,800 full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs in the UK, roughly equivalent to the entire NHS Wales FTE workforce.

Business schools have also been found to drive growth in every postcode, with the greatest economic impact noted in Coventry South, estimated at £432m, or £3,270 per resident.

Their significant contribution to the UK economy also highlights the global strength of the UK’s business and education offering.

Mainelli says the UK has the opportunity to allow “universities and business schools to recruit the top international students” competitors are “turning away.”

“There is a golden opportunity to get this right. Recruiting the best and brightest is not simply a tagline. It signals to the rest of the world that we are global leaders in higher education,” he added.

Declines will also have a knock-on effect on the future budget for maintenance grants, undermining the UK’s ability to meet the £40bn education exports set out in the international education strategy.

James Canning, principal consultant at London Economics, said the report highlighted the “positive impact” that international business school students have “not only on local economies, but also on the wider higher education sector.”

“The tuition fee income provided by international business school students is vital in a moment when close to half of the UK’s higher education providers face a deficit,” he said.

Not only do international business students contribute economically, they also advance the UK’s soft power and strengthen global trade links, with many going on to lead high-profile companies in the UK and around the world.

Notable alumni include Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou, founder, EasyJet (Bayes Business School), Aishah Ahmad, former deputy governor, Central Bank of Nigeria (Cranfield School of Management), Phuthi Mahanyele-Dabengwa, CEO, Naspers South Africa (Leicester Castle Business School), and Kumar Mangalam Birla, chairman, Aditya Birla Group (London Business School).

title: The view from Edinburgh: sustainable recruitment starts with sustainable partnerships
summary:
Sustainable recruitment is about more than maintaining student numbers or finding new markets, argues Stuart Easter. Building long-term international partnerships, investing in local expertise and embedding internationalisation across universities are crucial to creating recruitment strategies in an increasingly uncertain policy environment.

The post The view from Edinburgh: sustainable recruitment starts with sustainable partnerships appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
“Sustainable recruitment” has become one of the most frequently used phrases in the sector recently. It features prominently in the UK’s latest international education strategy (IES) and increasingly seems to shape conversations across universities, government departments and the wider sector.

Yet despite all the talk, I still don’t think there is a widely shared understanding across all stakeholders of what sustainable recruitment actually means.

For some, it is about financial sustainability. For others, maintaining enrolments from established markets. For government (and IES authors), it likely means ensuring international education remains politically and publicly sustainable. The challenge is that each definition captures only part of the picture.

Across the sector, changing immigration policies, geopolitical uncertainty, economic pressures and shifting student demand have shown how quickly long-standing recruitment patterns can change. What appears sustainable today may not be sustainable tomorrow.

At Edinburgh Napier University, that has increasingly led us to think about sustainability through the lens of partnership. Partnership with overseas organisations who support our enrolment work, as well as local organisations in Scotland that help students succeed during and after their studies.

For almost two decades, we have maintained a presence in Hyderabad, India. One lesson has remained constant: sustainable recruitment begins long before an application is submitted. Trusted partnerships, local knowledge and strong local networks require consistent investment, long-term commitment and a willingness to remain engaged beyond annual recruitment cycles.

This experience has also shaped our approach to diversification. Too often, diversification is viewed simply as identifying new recruitment markets. In reality, it requires investment in local expertise, regional understanding and relationships that extend beyond student recruitment.

One lesson has remained constant: sustainable recruitment begins long before an application is submitted

More broadly, internationalisation itself has become far more complex. International offices were traditionally measured largely through recruitment outcomes. International partnerships now encompass study abroad, articulation agreements, transnational education, research collaboration, employer engagement, alumni development and online learning.

As a result, the distinction between recruitment strategy and partnership strategy is becoming increasingly blurred. These relationships create value regardless of short-term fluctuations in student demand or policy settings.

At Edinburgh Napier University, this has meant strengthening our engagement across Europe and the Americas while continuing to invest in established markets. The objective has not been to react to short-term volatility but to build a broader and more balanced portfolio of international partnerships capable of supporting long-term resilience. This creates opportunities for wider engagement based around shared regional priorities and areas of institutional strength.

Europe also provides a useful example. Brexit fundamentally altered the UK’s relationship with European students and institutions, while renewed debate around EU fee status demonstrates how quickly policy environments can continue to evolve. Our partnerships have survived one major change, and will survive another.

Whatever the outcome of those discussions, they reinforce an important point: institutions cannot build international strategies around the expectation that policy environments will remain unchanged. Sustainable recruitment depends on relationships that retain value regardless of shifts in regulation, funding or student mobility patterns.

It also raises an important question. How much responsibility for sustainable recruitment should sit with university recruitment teams alone? Increasingly, international teams must become agents of change within their institutions. Sustainable recruitment depends not only on recruitment activity, but on the relevance of what universities offer students and partners. That may mean influencing portfolio development, partnership models, accommodation strategies, employer engagement and pathways into employment.

As the sector continues to explore what sustainable recruitment means in practice, we could start by recognising that sustainability is not always about maintaining the status quo.

It could also be about building the partnerships, capabilities and institutional resilience that allow universities to thrive when change inevitably comes. In that sense, sustainable recruitment is not primarily a recruitment challenge but an institutional one. Universities prepared to evolve alongside their partners will be best placed to succeed in an increasingly uncertain world.

About the author:

About the author: Stuart is chair of the British Universities’ International Liaison Association (BUILA) and director of global engagement at Edinburgh Napier University, where he is a member of the university senior leadership team. He oversees a team of over 50 staff in seven countries, with responsibility for all global engagement activity across recruitment, mobility and TNE in addition to a significant online distance learning operation.

Stuart has worked in higher education for over 15 years, including living and working in China and holding internationalisation, recruitment, and partnership development roles at three Scottish universities. He has previously served on Chevening scholarship reading committees and as a member of the Scottish Universities International Group committee and the Universities Scotland International Committee.

Elected to the BUILA Executive in 2021, Stuart currently serves at the organisation’s chair and oversees its LEAD pillar, focused on strengthening the association’s governance, organisational resilience, and capacity to deliver for members. His portfolio also includes director engagement, bringing senior colleagues together to share insight and inform BUILA’s strategic priorities.

title: Technology Enables Higher Ed IT Leaders to Make More Proactive Decisions
summary:
The higher education IT landscape has always been complex, but with distributed systems and governance structures, tight budgets and limited staff, technology decisions are often made in a vacuum. But as artificial intelligence proliferates throughout campus, cyberthreats intensify and classroom technology becomes more important than ever before, IT leaders are recognizing the need to be proactive. They are increasingly acting with intention, collaborating across departments to make decisions that will impact the entire campus community.
Click the banner below for tools to support a connected…
full_text:
Proactive Decision-Making Leads to Stronger Policies and Procedures

Everyone on campus wants to adopt AI, from back-office staff to faculty and students. To get a handle on AI tools, policies and governance, many institutions are establishing cross-departmental task forces to shape how the technology is used. These teams are helping to develop universal practices for adoption across an institution, so policies remain consistent and the IT team has visibility into the tools that are part of the campus ecosystem.

This visibility is extending to all third-party application providers. Higher education is no stranger to vendor data breaches, and security leaders are ramping up their risk management to ensure they can trust that their institutional information is safe. This means developing assessments that vendors must adhere to and procedures for how to act in case a breach does occur. These institutions are proactively addressing this risk to ensure they’re ready for anything.

In the classroom, rather than piecing together disparate audiovisual tools that work in a pinch, institutions are standardizing classroom design to ensure that no matter what room a faculty member enters, they will know how to operate the technology. This forward-thinking design strategy eliminates headaches for all parties and streamlines teaching and learning. And the device loaner initiatives implemented during the pandemic have evolved into thriving programs that make hardware available to students in need year-round.

Higher education institutions are pushing back against their pattern of improvised solutions, redundant technologies and reactive postures, and are opting to flesh out their policies and procedures and act with purpose. For an industry long defined by having to do more with less, doing things intentionally is most important.

Greetings from Plan, Act, Reflect & Eportfolio (PARE) from ePortfolios Australia. The idea is a group meet, in this case virtually, via Zoom. After introductions, you silently work on your portfolio, then discuss what you have written. This gives you permission to focus on your own writing, without interruption from other tasks. Some are working on their CVs for promotion, or applications for fellowships. In my case I decided to start on an idea I had for a second volume of writings, to follow Net Traveler, from 1999. I started to write a new introduction, but it is not very good. Then I asked Copilot to slect 20 articles, and make that a book.

My manual attempt:

Introduction

This is a sequel to my 1999 book “Net Traveller”, which was about how the Internet and the World Wide Web became a part of my everyday life. The Internet came to prominence at the end of my 19 year career working in government agencies on computer systems. I had come up through the ranks programming, ending up writing government tech policy. Wanting a new challenge, I left government to become an independent consultant, and part time academic. It did not quite work out that way, as I will relate in this selection of items. These consist, as with volume one, of edited versions of published material, during my last 26 years, helping companies, government agencies and universities.

During these decades I helped set the direction technology has taken. Rather than by writing policy, as previously, but by teaching, and helping with the direction of education in my profession. Along the way there was a pandemic, and upheaval in the university sector. While much was everyday routine, there were times it felt something momentous. An example was when if I was asked if I was coming to the emergency staff meeting (which I know nothing about). We were told the university faced an “existential threat”: a pandemic might kill us all, or put us out of business. We were asked could we immediately switch to teaching online. I hesitantly put up my hand and said “Yes. I have been trained to do that. I have a degree in it”.

As I write these words AI looms large. We have had an AI boom, and we are waiting to see if it is, as I suspect, a bubble. As in the past there is perhaps over optimism about technology, and a failure to understand the social factors.

This book, in large part, looks at how we can do university education better, not from theory, but from having done it.

title: Falscher Alarm: Bombendrohungen gegen Hunderte Schulen in Italien
summary: Nach Drohungen gegen den Flugverkehr und irische Medien trifft es jetzt Italiens Bildungseinrichtungen. Ministerpräsidentin Meloni spricht von einer Strategie, die Beunruhigung und Sorge schüren solle.
full_text:
In Italien sind am Mittwoch Hunderte Schulen evakuiert worden. Nach Medienberichten waren im ganzen Land in 312 Bildungseinrichtungen per E-Mail Bombendrohungen eingegangen, die sich bald als gegenstandslos herausstellten. Ministerpräsidentin Giorgia Meloni gab in einem Post auf ihrer Facebook-Seite Entwarnung: „Nach den bisher durchgeführten Überprüfungen gibt es keinerlei Hinweise, die auf eine konkrete Gefahr hindeuten würden.“ Es handele sich offenbar vielmehr um „eine Strategie, die darauf abzielt, Beunruhigung und Sorge zu schüren“. Meloni kündigte eine umfassende Untersuchung der Vorfälle an. Sie berief zudem eine Krisensitzung der Regierung ein.

Bildungsminister Giuseppe Valditara sagte im Fernsehen, es sei „nicht das erste Mal“ gewesen, dass es solche Drohungen gegeben habe. Die hohe Zahl der betroffenen Schulen zeige, „wie wenig wahrscheinlich eine wirkliche Bedrohung“ sei. „Wir müssen aber wachsam bleiben und uns zugleich bewusst machen, dass wir uns gegen eine hybride Kriegsführung, die von Staaten als Mittel zur Destabilisierung eingesetzt wird, wappnen müssen“, sagte der Minister.

Aus dem Inhalt der E-Mails gehe hervor, dass es sich „höchstwahrscheinlich um einen Cyberangriff und nicht um eine reale Bedrohung“ handele. Auch in Großbritannien und Irland gingen nach Polizeiangaben E-Mails mit ähnlichen Drohungen an Schulen ein. „Nichts deutet darauf hin, dass sie eine glaubhafte Bedrohung darstellen“, erklärte die Polizei.
